Oh wise gamers of whoaverse, lend me your wisdom. Ok, so I'm 16 and have never gamed before - my parents are super super strict and wouldn't buy me any sort of video game consoles; however, now that I have a job they've said that if that's what I want to buy they'll allow it as long as my grades don't fall. There are many gaming consoles out there and trying to figure out which one to buy, let alone good "starter" games is mind blowing! I'm basically just seeking advice here. Which gaming console is good for someone who has never really played video games before, other than at friends' houses, and which games would you recommend?
Also, I forgot to mention that I can spend about $300 - $450 right now (I will have a little bit more around $500 when I get paid again next week). Is this enough or do I need to save up more?

I'd go with a Nintendo Wii U. You get more bang for your buck. $299 - some bundled systems that come with a game are $329 depending. If you get the Wii U then get Mario Kart 8 before July 31st you get a free download game. If you're in the US there are four selections if in UK there are more. This of course is my biased opinion. Nintendo gets a lot of flak but they actually have REALLY fun and engaging games. Also, the Wii U is backward compatible with the Wii games so since you're new to gaming that opens up a ton of games for you to play since you've never played them before.

I'd say build a SteamOS rig, you'll learn about Linux and computer hardware. PC Part Picker should have most of the info you need to plan a build: http://pcpartpicker.com/ And once you've got it running there's TeamFortress2 for free, as well as the other free steam games. It won't be a beast of a computer. but for $500 something serviceable can be achieved, and a planned ram upgrade down the road could make $500 work for now with an easy upgrade for the future in sight.
Get a decent laptop that can run some popular games, I run bf3 on a refurb Asus I got off newegg for 390 last year. Plus because it's a laptop you may actually use it for school too.

Don't just listen to advice from randoms on the internet. Go try them!!!!

Saying that, I think you're possibly better off with an older console, maybe the 360 or the PS3? There's a massive back catalogue games etc should be cheap too.

Eventually upgrade to next gen or....maybe...get a PC? ;)

Don't buy a console. Buy a PC. Tell your parents you want to use it for gaming and working, they might like that. As for games, my favorite games of all time are Fallout: New Vegas and The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion, which are both amazing action/RPG titles. But if you don't like RPGs, keep trying other things, there are tons of games around. If you can afford it after you get a PC, a last-generation console (Xbox 360 or PlayStation 3) will be good, as the "next-gen" consoles don't have many good games.

get a cheap comp and some steam games, some good starter ones i can recommend are: The Elder Scrolls: Skyrim, GTA V, any Mario or Legend of Zelda game (might have to use an emulator), Portal, Left 4 Dead 2, Team Fortress 2 (it's free to play!), and N+.

If you'd like to get a console instead of a comp, I'd say go with a Wii or an Xbox 360, as they're older (so cheap), and have many games available for them.

So while it seems most people recommend building a PC, which is a good idea, you have another option as well. Get an old PS2 and a bunch of great old games really cheap. Personally I enjoy the many RPGs available on the platform such as the Final Fantasy series, Persona 4, among many others.

A PC or upgrade would be a really good idea.

A whole bunch of old console games have been ported to PC and there are just tonnes of great free games on PC.

Came here expecting PC gaming, and I wasn't let down.

I would say build a PC. Not only is it a learning experience, not only is the cost of gaming usually cheaper, not only are mods basically non-existent...But a PC is something that is constant. It isn't a single use machine that you upgrade when Sony and Microsoft tell you to. It isn't a single format, non-customizeable piece of hardware that is locked to Microsoft or Sony.

That being said...building a PC isn't for everyone and in your budget buying a pre-built one isn't a great option. The upcharge you pay on any pre-built is so high it is taking you of the price range of a decent rig. Also, if you can get some hands on time with a mouse and keyboard as well as a controller and see which one you like best...and I don't mean ten minutes. Mouse and keyboard takes more getting used to but once you're accustomed to it, most people prefer it because of the precision it gives you...not to mention you can just use a regular controller on a PC anyhow but not every game supports it and relying on 3rd party software can be a pain.

either way, you're looking at most of your money going to the actual platform itself...whether it be a console or a PC...and if that is the case then you can usually find games online for far cheaper than you can in-store so you'd be able to dive into more games sooner. Also, as i said before, having a PC and knowing how to assemble and run it yourself is invaluable knowledge in a world where technology is ever increasing.
"The key difference between alternative medicine and evidence-based medicine"

It's often said by healthcare practitioners that if alternative "medicine" worked, it would be called "medicine." I am 100% in agreement with this and think that the internet has done quite a bit of damage to evidence-based medicine. The idea that a patient goes into a doctors office, tells the doctor their diagnosis (without any sort of expert assessment or history), and then dictates to the doctor the correct course of treatment is, well, absurd.

Doctors spend 4 years in medical school and another few years in a residency program (2 - 5+ depending on specialty). They have not only the textbook knowledge, but the clinical experience to diagnose and treat whereas someone with access to google has maybe a few hours of research completed. BIG DIFFERENCE. Do doctors get their diagnoses wrong sometimes, hell yes, but that's why there are second opinions. Wikipedia is not a good alternative to a medical doctor who has treated countless numbers of patients.

This blog does a pretty good job of laying out the difference between alternative "medicine" and evidence-based medicine.
